questions.question: What's actually gained by searching for a formal proof instead of just running the program on many cases, if both cost unbounded effort?

passages.quote: we don’t get any fundamental advantage by trying to make a proof rather than just running the Turing machine

questions.question: Does this mean any program that actually does something computationally worthwhile is doomed to carry some risk of bugs?

passages.quote: to make the program worth actually running, there have to be parts of its behavior you can’t foresee
it’s very common for programs to have what amounts to a “spark of computational irreducibility inside”

questions.question: If computational irreducibility makes a program's behavior unforeseeable short of running it, how can any formal proof of correctness ever succeed?

passages.quote: there will always be certain things about a system that one will be able to predict
One can think of proofs as taking advantage of pockets of computational reducibility, to provide finite summaries of infinite things.

questions.question: Since scientific induction works in physics but fails in biology, does this tell us anything about how reliable induction should be for software behavior?

passages.quote: insofar as the details of what programs do matters, one’s going to have the potential to run into computational irreducibility

questions.question: Given that math can encode arbitrary computation (per Gödel), why doesn't pure mathematics suffer the same flood of unexpected 'bugs' as ruliology?

passages.quote: pure mathematics as it’s normally practiced tends to concentrate on what amount to more “human-level” questions, that in effect exist in pockets of computational reducibility

questions.question: If a well-designed language pushes irreducibility into its primitives, does that mean programs written in it can be made completely bug-free?

passages.quote: any time you write a program that actually needs to be written (in the sense that it’s achieving at least some irreducible computation), it’ll have the possibility of doing something you didn’t expect

questions.question: If AI is good at catching bugs that follow familiar human mistakes, can it also be expected to catch the deeper, irreducibility-driven bugs discussed here?

passages.quote: modern AIs are typically quite good at finding bugs that follow the patterns of typical human missteps
What we’ve mostly discussed here are, however, what amount to deeper kinds of bugs. They are bugs that do not follow any human-related patterns.

questions.question: For systems like modern neural networks that don't have an obvious visual 'spacetime' picture, is there any way to actually see inside and rule out surprises?

passages.quote: What actually happens in a realistic neural net will be very hard to visualize or to “understand at a human level”

questions.question: Does allowing some bugs actually let a program be made shorter, or is that only true for low-level code like Turing machines rather than well-designed languages?

passages.quote: if our program is written at a lower level, say as a Turing machine, then we can expect (as we saw above) that allowing some bugs can allow the program to be shorter
